title: RPT-UPDATE 2-Vietnam to allow gold imports to stabilise market
text:
(Repeats from Wednesday without changes)

 * Vietnam relaxes gold ban in place since May '08

 * No volume limit, but only 5 or 6 firms can import  (Updates with details)

 By John Ruwitch and Ho Binh Minh

 HANOI, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Vietnam's central bank on Wednesday lifted a 1-1/2-year-old ban on gold imports in a bid to stabilise the market after a sharp rise in prices helped drive the country's dong currency to a record low.

 "The State Bank of Vietnam will allow gold imports with a volume sufficient to intervene in the market in order to stabilise the market, combat speculation and prevent an impact on the interests of the people," the central bank said on its Web site, www.sbv.gov.vn("http://www.sbv.gov.vn").

 Five or six companies would be allowed to import unlimited quantities of gold, state-run news Web site VNexpress.net quoted State Bank of Vietnam Governor Nguyen Van Giau as saying on Wednesday afternoon.

 He did not give details or a timeframe.

 The ban on gold imports since May 2008 led to a gap between domestic and international prices, and recently traders say that spread, plus the rise in gold prices globally, triggered a surge in demand for dollars.

 "This morning the prices and the market went crazy, the worst time in my 20 years of trading," an owner of a gold shop in Hanoi's downtown district of Hoan Kiem said.

 "Prices collapsed this afternoon and the decision on gold imports will certainly help control the situation."

 By early afternoon on Wednesday the dong hit 19,800 per dollar -- about 7 percent lower than the rate a week ago -- before rebounding to around 19,000.

 For a Q+A on the currency, click: [ID:nHAN491590]

 Gold leapt above 29 million dong per tael on Wednesday, or $1,261 per troy ounce at an exchange rate of 19,000 dong per dollar. Later it deflated to around 27.5 million dong. Last Wednesday it was at about 24.5 million dong per tael.

 Internationally, gold <XAU=> has gained more than 25 percent in 2009, driven by persistent weakness in the U.S. dollar, expectations of more buying from central banks and fears about the health of the global economy.

 It shot to a record high at $1,117.05 an ounce on Wednesday as the dollar slipped to its lowest in more than a year, lifting bullion's appeal as an alternative investment.

 TURNING AWAY CUSTOMERS

 The government responded to the price spikes earlier in the day by dispatching inspectors to gold shops, which double as foreign exchange changers, dealers said.

Central bank rules allow the dong to trade with the dollar within a band of 5 percent on either side of a reference rate it sets each day. A rate of 19,800 dong per dollar is more than triple the limit.

 By early afternoon, gold and currency quotes were brought back down but some shops were turning away walk-in customers. The central bank blamed domestic speculators for pushing the gold price above world levels.

 Offshore dealers covering Vietnam said gold bars had been smuggled in from neighbouring countries to meet growing demand.

 "The thing is, people are cautious," a dealer in Singapore said. "The domestic price is so high because they haven't imported gold for a long time. Basically, there's a shortage of physical gold."

 Vietnam consumed 115.8 tonnes of gold for jewellery and investment in 2008, up from 77.5 tonnes in 2007.

 Traditionally, the Vietnamese use gold for savings, jewellery and real estate transactions but when inflation is high, many choose gold or the U.S. dollar to hedge against inflation.  (Additional reporting by Lewa Pardomuan in Singapore; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

title: UPDATE 2-Vietnam to let dong dip 3 pct vs dollar on Dec 25
text:
(Adds quotes, background)

HANOI, Dec 24 (Reuters) - Vietnam's central bank will let the dong fall 3 percent against the dollar from Dec. 25 in interbank transactions, a state-run newspaper quoted Governor Nguyen Van Giau as saying on Wednesday.

The mid-point will be 16,988 dong per dollar on Thursday, from 16,494 dong on Wednesday, while the daily trading band remains unchanged at 3 percent either side of the mid-point, Giau was quoted by the Vietnam Economic Times newspaper as saying.

The State Bank of Vietnam's mid-point quote on Reuters <SBOV> late on Wednesday was 16,989 for Dec. 25.

The dong could fall to 17,497 per dollar on Thursday in interbank quotations, from 16,989 dong per dollar on Wednesday, Giau told a news conference in Ho Chi Minh City, to which foreign media were not invited.

The mid-point intervention on Thursday by the State Bank of Vietnam is the second this year after it allowed the rate to drop 2 percent in June. So far, the dong has fallen roughly 6 percent against the dollar this year on the interbank market.

The government has told the central bank "to flexibly adjust the exchange rate following market signals, encourage exports, control imports, stabilise the macroeconomy and strive to manage the international balance of payment without facing a deficit," Giau said.

The devaluation was not expected.

The interbank dollar/dong market has been frozen for weeks, with the dong stuck at the weak end of its band and almost no deals being done. Banks say they have been rationing dollars for long-term or special customers.

"Trade and investment flows have been negative, putting selling pressure on the dong, and recent bouts of inflation have also conspired to drive the currency's value lower," said Michael Woolfolk, senior currency strategist at Bank of New York Mellon.

"The decision today merely reflects the supply and demand conditions that have built up in recent weeks."

In the past two weeks bankers in Vietnam had said the market was expecting the central bank to widen the band to 4 or 5 percent, which would effectively allow the dong to depreciate.

"This is more or less good news," a trader at a major Vietnamese bank said. "It will make it a little bit easier for the market to move, but it is not going to make things any better in the long term. ... I think the market is going to hit the ceiling soon."

Vietnam has had a rough year. It battled double-digit inflation and a widening trade deficit in the first two quarters by tightening monetary policy, but with inflation starting to ease authorities have pulled out the stops to offset the dampening effect of the global credit crisis on growth.

The central bank last month for the third time this year widened the daily band in which the dong is allowed to move, increasing it to 3 percent either side of a fixed mid-point set each day, from 2 percent.

Vietnam estimated its trade deficit this year would grow 20.6 percent to $17 billion, below earlier government forecasts, as exports jumped 29.5 percent, the highest growth since 2004, a state-run newspaper reported on Wednesday.

Economists at a coffee conference this month said that the dong could be devalued next year due to a worsening balance of payments and bad bank debts while the government also needed to prop up exports hit by the global economic downturn.

The dollar/dong exchange rate should have been lowered to 17,000 dong or 18,000 dong per dollar, an economist told Reuters at the conference. (Additional reporting by John Ruwitch in Hanoi and Daniel Bases in New York; Editing by Jonathan Oatis)

title: ANALYSIS-Vietnam's  forex  market to stay frozen for now
text:
HANOI, Dec 23 (Reuters) - Vietnam's tightly-regulated foreign exchange market may have broken down completely with the authorities reluctant to let the currency significantly depreciate but unable to prop it up by intervention.

The dong <VND=> has been glued to the weak end of its central bank-mandated trading band against the dollar for several weeks and traders say there have been almost no deals.

"From the outside, it looks like the currency's stable," said Tim Condon, chief economist at ING Financial Markets in Singapore. "But what you're not seeing is that the market really has kind of broken down."

Banks have been rationing dollars for long-term customers and key clients, turning away others. Currency traders say little is being done to un-stick what HSBC has estimated to be about $300 million a day market in normal times.

These days, one local bank that said it normally did several dozen deals a day was down to a couple, at best, and foreign banks that did fewer in normal times are doing basically none.

This may be the price authorities are willing to pay for a stable exchange rate at the end of a turbulent year.

Economic overheating fuelled by soaring inflation and a widening trade deficit pushed the offshore non-deliverable forwards fix to price the dong at more than 19,000 per dollar <VNDFIX=ABSG> in June, around 12 percent weaker than the spot rate at the time. The offshore fix is what foreign bankers take as the best gauge of the dong's market value.

Fearing an all-out run on the dong in June, the State Bank of Vietnam cracked down on the black market. Then it banned banks from using currencies such as the euro, which were exempt from exchange controls, as proxies to trade dollar/dong.

To circumvent the daily exchange rate against the dollar, banks had asked local dollar buyers to buy the euro, and then convert the euro to dollars using international rates to arrive at the amount of dong they have to pay.

The crackdown worked and exchange rates snapped back, but the numbers being quoted are not true market clearing rates.

"All banks keep asking for bids, not offers, because the price is already at the ceiling," said Lai Tat Ha, deputy manager of treasury at Techcombank.

"The market now is not about rates, it's about liquidity."

The central bank's options are limited.

"If you enforce the band, you have to let the market operate within the band, which means you have to widen the band or intervene," said a senior banker at a foreign bank in Hanoi, who did not want to be named because he was not authorised to speak to the media.

Bankers suspect Vietnam lacks the muscle to defend its currency through intervention. The central bank does not regularly publish foreign exchange reserves, but governor Nguyen Van Giau estimated that at the end of September it had about $21.9 billion. That figure was smaller than the reserves of any Asian country that publishes data, except Bangladesh and Pakistan.

BAND WIDENING

Investors are betting the trading band will be expanded soon from the 3 percent that the dong is allowed to rise or fall from midpoint rate set by the central bank each day. Forward contracts were pricing a 13 percent dong depreciation in a year and a 4 percent drop in three months <PNDG>.

The band has been widened three times so far this year, from three-quarters of a percent to the current 3 percent. More widening will not be a panacea.

"It will make a little difference to the extent that people who are keeping dollars will sell, but that is not going to make the market any better in the long term," said Techcombank's Ha.

The dong would quickly be sucked to the weak end of the new band, and policymakers would be stuck in the same fix: trading liquidity for exchange rate stability in the hope that depreciation pressures will ease, or can be managed, before serious harm is done to the economy.

Already, economists have taken a machete to Vietnam's gross domestic product growth forecast for next year as an economic boom driven by flows of foreign capital crumbles. The government is forecasting 6-6.5 percent growth, and the IMF is looking at 5 percent. Last year, the economy grew 8.5 percent.

It remains to be seen whether the gamble will pay off. Foreign capital is unlikely to return until the government restores confidence in the foreign exchange market.

Economists at a coffee conference earlier this month said they think Vietnam may have to devalue next year, and say the dong should trade between 17,000-18,000 per dollar [ID:nHAN401110].

Currently, it is officially just shy of 17,000, while the NDF fix has slipped to around 17,200, its weakest since June.

But time may be on policymakers' side. The latest spell of U.S. dollar's weakness has been a windfall.

The dong came under pressure, along with most emerging market currencies, when the dollar rallied to 10-week highs against the euro and other major currencies as investors retreated from risky assets in the face of the financial crisis.

Now the dollar is back in the doldrums and the index that tracks the dollar against major currencies is down 6.5 percent this month.

"Demand for the dollar from both speculators and importers has been weakening significantly because the currency has depreciated against others such as the euro and the yen, we are sitting on a lot of unsold dollars right now," said one manager of a major gold shop that trades forex.

And three traders said some Vietnamese banks have started quietly using third currencies again to circumvent the dollar/dong band. None of them agreed to be identified because of the sensitivity of the information.

The central bank has said forex stability is a goal for next year and the appearance of stability should be welcomed in a highly dollarised economy that had an inflation scare this year, which peaked at an annual rate of 28.3 percent in August.

"There will be a cost to what's happened this year," Condon said. "Obviously, the authorities would like to minimise that... This is probably a case of time healing the wounds." (Additional reporting by Nguyen Nhat Lam; Editing by Dayan Candappa)

title: INTERVIEW- Vietnam  c.bank says dong stable, not  intervening
text:
HANOI, July 25 (Reuters) - Vietnam's central bank said on Friday the domestic foreign exchange market had stabilised, supply and demand of dong was balanced, and it had not intervened in the dong market since early June. State Bank of Vietnam Deputy Governor Nguyen Van Binh also said the central bank had not placed any restrictions on foreign exchange transactions by exporters or importers, nor had it restrained the black market.

He declined comment on Vietnam's interest rates policy.

"We did not make any control on the black market because the black market is out of our control," Binh told Reuters on the sidelines of an event.

"We made some tightening policy regarding our foreign exchange bureau in order to correct the activities within the regulations of the central bank."

The dong <VND=>, one of Asia's least convertible currencies, has steadied this month in a 16,500-16,850 per dollar range. Traders believe the central bank's intervention and its measures to cool bank lending have helped improve sentiment among investors who at one point in June were pricing in a 30 percent depreciation in the currency within 12 months.

Rates in black market deals, in which local Vietnamese illicitly convert their dong into dollars, have also changed. These dollars are now available at close to the official rate, rather than the 13-15 percent premium they used to command in June.

Binh, who's in charge of foreign exchange, said the central bank had intervened between the end of March until early June to stabilise the dong, but he declined to divulge how much had been spent on such intervention.

"We have stopped intervening," Binh said.

"We did not use foreign exchange reserves so far. We intervened only on the basis of the amount of foreign exchange that we purchased from the market," he said.

Vietnam does not regularly report its foreign reserves data but a finance ministry official said in June the country's reserves totalled $20.7 billion.

Responding to a question on whether there would be changes to Vietnam's policy of allowing the dong to move in a 2 percent band around a daily mid-point, and whether the central bank wanted to see the currency weaken, he said:

"In general our policy is that we keep the exchange rate stable but not fixed. We keep it stable but we are flexible to changes in the market."

With annual inflation running at 27 percent and after a hefty fuel price rise this week, economists and investors expect the central bank to raise rates for the fourth time this year. (Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Neil Fullick)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia down on Fed outlook, Vietnam cuts dong
text:
SINGAPORE, June 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on Wednesday after remarks by U.S. officials fanned expectations of higher U.S. interest rates this year, while Vietnam cut the official dong rate in what analysts described as an effective devaluation.

The Thai baht <THB=TH> fell as far as 33.18 per dollar, down nearly 0.7 percent from late Asian trade on Tuesday. Suspected central bank intervention to support the currency helped keep it above a five-month low of 33.41 hit on Monday.

Traders attributed th baht's weakness to the dollar's broad strength and expected the baht to move in tight ranges as the Bank of Thailand has been intervening in currency markets to support the baht.

"They (the central bank) have been in the market since 33.1-33.13 this morning," said a Bangkok-based trader.

Central banks in South Korea, the Philippines, India, and Indonesia have also sold dollars in recent sessions to limit the declines in their currencies out of concern that further weakness could stoke inflationary risks.

"We view regional central bank action as consistent with the anti-inflation bias of monetary policy and expect continued policy action to stabilise the markets," JPMorgan strategists Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho said in a note.

The dollar hit a 3-1/2-month high versus the yen <JPY=> and held gains against the euro <EUR=> after more U.S. officials talked tougher on inflation, cementing expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates later this year.

Dallas Fed President Richard Fisher said on Tuesday the U.S. central bank would not allow inflation expectations to rise unchecked, echoing comments made by Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke a day earlier. [ID:nN10365737]

The warnings about inflation came amid a barrage of remarks from U.S. officials saying they are keeping an eye on the U.S. currency while leaving options open for dollar-buying intervention to stem its slide. [ID:nN10365737]

VIETNAM CUTS DONG RATE

Vietnam's central bank cut the dong by almost 2 percent against the dollar on Wednesday to a record low in what analysts described as an effective devaluation of the currency after inflation in the country surged to 25 percent in May.

Some analysts have warned about a possible currency crisis in Vietnam as the offshore non-deliverable forwards now imply a nearly 30 percent plunge in the dong's value in the next year.

"Vietnam is the closest to a crisis but the conditions that brought it there are present elsewhere," said Tim Condon, head of Asia research at ING.

"We consider Indonesia and the Philippines the most vulnerable to contagion from Vietnam," he said in a note.

Rising inflation has taken a toll on the South Korean won <KRW=>, the Philippines peso <PHP=> and Indian rupee <INR=IN>. These three currencies have fallen against the dollar so far this year, while other Asian currencies are firmer.

The peso fell as much as a fifth of a percent on Wednesday to 44.50 per dollar, its weakest level since October.

The won lost nearly 0.4 percent to 1,030 per dollar, but the rupee edged up to 42.857 per dollar amid expectations that foreign investors may resume buying of local shares.

Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.3740 per U.S. dollar at one point, down half of a percent.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> retreated as far as 6.9252 per dollar from its post-revaluation high of 6.9140 hit on Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 1-Vietnam says no plans for  currency  devaluation
text:
(Adds details, market rates, comments)

 HANOI, June 6 (Reuters) - Vietnam's government has no plans to devalue the dong in spite of the forwards markets pricing in a sharp depreciation in the value of the currency one year from now, the country's second-largest bank BIDV said on Friday.

 The government also has sufficient foreign currency reserves to meet investors' demands to convert their funds into dollars, Prime Minister Nguyen Tan Dung was quoted as saying in the bank's statement.

 Vietnam will strive to reduce its inflation to single digits by 2010, Dung told BIDV Chairman Tran Bac Ha and JPMorgan's Head of Economic and Sovereign Research, David Fernandez, at a meeting on Thursday, BIDV said.

 Vietnam's economy and the dong are under pressure from inflation running at more than 25 percent and rising imports.

 The country's overall balance of payments for the first five months of the year was a surplus $1 billion, Dung said.

 "Given the current forex surplus, the prime minister believed that the dollar/dong trading band should be adjusted in a flexible manner in both directions," the statement quoted Dung as saying of the current daily band of +/-1 percent.

 In the short term, the band could be changed to come close to the +/- 2 percent as projected by the government, he said.

 Analysts said the remarks would help calm market jitters over recent volatility.

 "I think the market has seen some dramatic moves (in Vietnam) recently, and the comments are aimed at trying to calm down the market's nerves over how policy makers are dealing with the inflation problem," said David Mann, currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong.

 "We are expecting more of a smooth weakening of the dong than the NDF market suggests -- some market expectations do appear to be overdone."

 VOLATILITY

 Earlier on Friday, BIDV called on the central bank to take more action to stabilise the dong as it fell to fresh lows under pressure from rising import prices [ID:nHAN269583].

 In offshore non-deliverable forwards <PNDG>, the dong firmed to 22,800/23,800 per dollar on one-year term by 0848 GMT, implying the currency will be worth around 30 percent less in a year's time.

 The dong's <VND=> spot rate was at 16,283/16,285 per dollar.

 Dung said offshore markets which priced in a fall of between 20 and 40 percent in forwards deals had no grounds doing so.

 He said the State Bank of Vietnam would step up its measures to intervene in the markets.

 "The government will soon publish its foreign exchange reserves in dollars," the BIDV statement said, adding that Dung has asked the State Bank of Vietnam to publish the reserves on a regular basis to win the public's trust.

 Dung assured the two bankers at the meeting that Vietnam would not conduct any policy to control foreign portfolio investments, which would contravene the country's commitments toward integration and the market economy it pursues.

 Mann of Standard Chartered said rising oil prices have had a major impact on the economy and inflation was likely to climb.

 "We are still expecting inflation, which is quite high right now, to go even higher in the third quarter," Mann said. "But we think it will start coming off by the fourth quarter and the first quarter of next year."

 (Reporting by Ho Binh Minh and Kevin Yao, editing by Jacqueline Wong)

title: Vietnam Money- Central bank  seen stabilising rates.
text:
HANOI, March 24 (Reuters) - Facing a weakened dollar on growing concerns that the U.S.-led war in Iraq could take longer than some had expected, Vietnam's central bank is expected to intervene to keep exchange rates stable to boost exports. 

 "The central bank will have to step in if things get out of control," said a banker at a local bank in Hanoi on Monday. 

Central bank deputy governor Phung Khac Ke was quoted on Monday by Dau Tu (Investment) newspaper as saying that the bank would be "flexible in regulating foreign exchange operations to secure support for exports" in case the war in Iraq drags on. 

 Last month, Vietnam raised its export growth for 2003 to $18.5 billion from $18 billion set late last year by the National Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, after exports in 2002 rose 10 percent year-on-year to $16.53 billion. 

 The dollar fell against most major currencies on Monday including the euro and the yen on fear a prolonged war would pressure an already expanding fiscal deficit and undermine the greenback. 

 Apart from the possible negative impact of a weakened dollar, the U.S.-led strike on Iraq is taking a toll on local exporters. 

 Vietnam shipped $500 million of annual agricultural exports to Iraq last year. Shipments were cancelled or put on hold after the United States launched its attack on Iraq last Thursday. 

 "Demand for the dong has already firmed up as businesses move into implementation and disbursement stage of their projects," said Pham Van Thang, director of Habubank branch in Hanoi whose main clients are from the private sector. 

 DONG DEMAND STRONG 

 "So far companies are still on an expansionary track so the demands for the dong will be strong," Thang added. 

 Besides the private sector's growing needs for loans in the local currency, the demand for the dong is principally for funding major projects including the building of the north-south highway, a $1.3 billion oil refinery and several power plants, bankers noted. 

 "Strong domestic demand for the dong will help offset the impact of a weakening of the dollar on the dollar-dong exchange rates," said a financial expert in Hanoi. 

 On Monday, the central bank set the dong at 15,414 against the dollar, eight points higher from a week ago. 

 Despite signs of a weakening dollar, local bankers said they are sticking to the forecast that the dong would devalue by three percent against the dollar this year, compared with 2.1 percent in 2002. 

 Meanwhile, rates of short-term dong loans on the tiny interbank market have gone back down to the level two weeks ago, with overnight loans this week at 4.50-5.00 percent, against 4.50-5.25 percent last week. 

 Banks also raised interest rates on gold deposits following a recent fall in world gold prices. State media said the Bank for Exports and Imports (Eximbank) has added a 0.3 percentage point to its annual interest rates on gold deposits for all terms. 

 Its rate on the 12-month deposits now stands at 3.90 percent, said the Vietnam Economic Times newspaper. 

 Vietnam produces less than two tonnes of gold per year and imports between 35 and 40 tonnes for local consumption. Domestic gold prices eased to $315.49 an ounce on Monday from $323.88 last Wednesday. ($1=15,414 dong).

title: Vietnam  Central Bk  Intervened  To Stabilize Dong - Report
text:
HANOI, Vietnam (AP-Dow Jones)--Vietnam's central bank injected millions of U.S. dollars into money markets in an effort to stabilize the dong after it's continued drop in black market trading, official media reported Monday. 

 The bank's deputy governor, Le Duc Thuy, told reporters the Vietnamese currency would level off at about 12,300 dong against the dollar, the official Saigon Times Daily reported. 

 The State Bank of Vietnam earlier this month effectively devalued the dong, by expanding the trading band within which it can fluctuate against the dollar and other currencies. 

 Within days of the move, the dong had dropped from about 11,600 per dollar to 13,200 at some black market trading houses. 

 The devaluation was prompted by Southeast Asia's regional currency crisis. Vietnam's artificially inflated dong was driving export prices up compared with neighboring competitors. 

 Although the expanded plus or minus 10% trading band officially allows the dong to drop to about 12,300 against the dollar, black market trading drove the price even lower. 

 'The change was essentially of a psychological nature,' Thuy was quoted as telling the state-run Vietnam News Agency. 

 Thuy said Vietnam's reserves were plentiful enough to limit the fallout on the dong and stabilize both dollar and gold prices. 

 In the first 10 days after the dong's trading band was expanded, the state bank sold about $75 million to various commercial banks, the newspaper reported.

title: Vietnam  Ctrl Bk/Trading Band -2:Will  Intervene  If Necessary
text:
HO CHI MINH CITY, Vietnam (Dow Jones)--Vietnam's central bank, the State Bank of Vietnam, has no plans to widen the dong's trading band again, or dramatically adjust the central rate set daily by the bank governor's office, a State Bank official told Dow Jones Wednesday. 

 The official, who declined to be named, said, 'We have no plans in the coming times to adjust the target rate.' 

 His comments followed the central bank's move Monday to widen the trading band to plus or minus 10% from the central rate, which widened the band from the previous band of plus or minus 5% that had been in place since March. 

 The official said the move was to 'help the buyer and seller to meet each other.' 

 The State Bank's move Monday contradicted repeated bank statements that it would not widen the band. 

 Bankers and economists had called for a weaker dong in light of the current spate of regional currency devaluations. Vietnamese officials had said they were worried about Vietnam's export competitiveness, given the competition from the country's Asian neighbors. 

 Vietnam's trade deficit was $4.0 billion in 1996, and the government hopes to narrow it to $3.3 billion in 1997. 

 The official, who works in State Bank of Vietnam Deputy Governor Le Duc Thuy's office, said that the central bank will intervene to support the dong if it is necessary for the economy. 

 'We will support the currency to stabilize the exchange rate and benefit the economy,' he said. 

 The official declined to confirm media reports that Vietnam's foreign reserves stand at $2.5 billion, or enough to cover 10 weeks of imports. 

 In Vietnam, such information is a 'state secret,' he said. 

 Wednesday, the State Bank set the target rate for the dong at 11,171 dong to the dollar, up from Tuesday's 11,176 dong to the dollar. After the bank was widened, the dong fell to the floor of the band, and has remained there ever since. 

 At late afternoon, the dollar stood at 12,250 dong in very thin trade. Bankers said traders aren't willing to sell dollars at these levels because they're hoping for a further depreciation. 

 (END) DOW JONES ASIAN EQUITIES REPORT  15-10-97

title: FOCUS - Thai package leaves SE Asian  currencies  cold.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Thailand's eagerly awaited financial reform package provoked scarcely a sound in Southeast Asian currency markets on Tuesday as traders found little cause for celebration. 

 The Thai baht drifted slightly lower in offshore markets after easing on afternoon rumours that Thailand would lift its two-tier exchange rate system as part of the reform package. 

 "It's the same old crap we've seen for so long. That's probably why the dollar/baht is a bit higher now because most of the offshore players are disappointed," said a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore. 

 He said the baht's downside would be limited to 36.80 in offshore markets. It was at 36.10/40 to the dollar offshore at 1030 GMT against 35.90/36.00 six hours earlier. The onshore rate was little changed at 36.45/55. 

 Thai officials announced measures, including legislation to create two agencies to restructure and manage suspended Thai finance firms, requirements for financial institutions to raise their capital and amendments to bankruptcy laws. 

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said Thailand had no plans to close any more financial institutions in addition to the 58 finance firms already suspended. 

 On Monday, Thailand relaxed conditions for the 58 finance firms to resume business, increasing the time allowed them to repay a combined 430 billion baht borrowed from the central bank from three years to eight. 

 "From the looks of it, there's nothing new. The reaction came before the release of the package on the rumours about the two-tier market," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst at I.D.E.A. 

 Other Southeast Asian currencies remained within earlier ranges, trading mainly on domestic factors. 

 The Singapore dollar hit a low of 1.5440 to the U.S. dollar after Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the country would not emerge unhurt from the regional currency crisis. 

 It recovered to 1.5384/94 to the U.S. dollar, near its opening levels but off an early high of around 1.5300. 

 "The reaction was a bit overdone because interbank and short-term players were just focusing on the one-liner, but his whole talk dealt with globalisation of markets," said Ishaq. 

 He said U.S. fund buying of the Malaysian ringgit against the Singapore dollar, in a reversal of earlier positions, had contributed to the Singapore dollar's drop. 

 The ringgit remained relatively firm at 3.1060/1110 to the U.S. dollar from an opening around 3.14 on local corporate demand ahead of the Malaysian budget on Friday. 

 Dealers said there was speculation Malaysian state oil firm Petronas may be behind some of the ringgit purchases through a large Malaysian bank. A Petronas spokesman declined comment. 

 The ringgit was expected to keep to a 3.08-3.20 range before the budget. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was sandwiched between domestic corporate demand for dollars below the 3,450 rupiah level and talk of central bank intervention around 3,500. 

 "The central bank appeared around 3,490 and sold a token amount of dollars, probably less than $50 million," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The rupiah was at 3,470/3,500 to the dollar against an opening 3,450/3,500. Dealers said the market would be cautious before more details of the International Monetary Fund's aid programme for Indonesia became available. 

 The Philippine peso ended down at 34.13 to the dollar after thrice breaching its volatility band, causing it to be confined to a 31.514-34.139 band for the rest of the session. 

 Manila traders said the peso's weakness was sparked by companies buying dollars to cover foreign exchange exposure. The central bank also failed to put up a strong defence after intervening early in the day. 

Vietnam's non-convertible dong became the latest victim of the regional currency rout as the central bank widened the permitted trading band to 10 percent either side of the official daily rate from five percent, allowing it room to slide.
